title: Four product families, one connectivity layer
body:
## The architecture of a connectivity layer

Astera Labs has never broken out revenue by product family in its SEC disclosures, and the FY2025 10-K filed in February 2026 did not change that practice. The company reports a single revenue line. What it has disclosed — through management commentary on earnings calls, the product-family architecture described on asteralabs.com, and the implicit weighting of how Chief Product Officer Casey Morrison and CEO Jitendra Mohan allocate public attention — is that four silicon families constitute the business: Aries, Taurus, Leo, and Scorpio. Each addresses a different bottleneck in the AI server rack. Together they represent a deliberate bet that the AI infrastructure buildout would be won at the connectivity layer, not at the GPU or the accelerator, and that whoever designed the highest-performance path between components would capture the margin that typically accrues to the most constrained piece of any system.

The FY2025 result — $852.5M of revenue, 75.7% GAAP gross margin, $219.1M GAAP net income — validates the theory at scale. Understanding how the four families fit together is the foundation for assessing whether it continues to hold.

## Aries: the retimer as required component

The original Astera Labs product and, by all available evidence, the dominant revenue contributor through FY2025, Aries is the company's line of PCIe and CXL retimers and smart retimers. Its strategic logic begins with a physical fact: as PCIe link rates have advanced from Gen4 to Gen5 and now Gen6, the signal integrity requirements on server board traces have moved beyond what passive copper can reliably carry across the distances demanded by modern multi-socket AI server designs. A retimer regenerates and retimes the SerDes signals, restoring the eye diagram that passive attenuation degrades. At PCIe Gen5 speeds — 32 GT/s per lane — and certainly at Gen6's 64 GT/s — retimers transitioned from an optional design element to a mandatory one.

This transition is the structural tailwind that drove Astera's revenue from $396.3M in FY2024 to $852.5M in FY2025. Aries retimers sit on the path between every AI accelerator GPU and its host CPU in a modern AI server, and as hyperscalers and OEMs qualified Gen5 platforms through 2024 and into the Nvidia Blackwell and Blackwell-Ultra ramp of 2025, volume followed qualification. The 18-to-24-month design-in cycle that Astera has described as characteristic of its go-to-market meant that positions won in Hopper-generation qualification programs began generating revenue as Blackwell slots filled the quarterly production schedule.

The "smart" variant of Aries — the smart retimer — adds embedded monitoring and management capability to the basic signal-regeneration function, providing hyperscalers and OEMs with per-link visibility that simplifies both initial bring-up and in-field diagnostics. The value proposition of the smart variant is incremental per unit but compounds across a rack of hundreds or thousands of retimer slots, and it supports a higher ASP that contributes to the margin structure discussed below.

The competitive surface on Aries runs primarily against Broadcom and Microchip, both of which have retimer product lines. Astera's pricing power — sustained at 75.7% GAAP gross margin across a full fiscal year — implies the company has not been materially price-competed out of its hyperscaler design-ins, which is consistent with the switching-cost mechanics of a 18-24 month requalification cycle.

## Taurus: smart cable modules and the rack interconnect layer

Where Aries addresses the within-server signal path, Taurus addresses the between-rack interconnect at the 200G, 400G, and 800G Ethernet speeds that AI cluster traffic now demands. The product is the Ethernet Smart Cable Module — a module that combines the physical cable medium with embedded link-management and monitoring silicon. The "smart" positioning is the key differentiator from passive Direct Attach Copper or conventional Active Optical Cable alternatives: Taurus modules carry Astera-designed silicon that provides per-link telemetry, fault isolation, and link management at speeds where passive options cannot reliably meet BER requirements at the link lengths AI rack designs demand.

Taurus occupies the second tier of Astera's revenue contribution based on management commentary and the product family's position in earnings-call narratives. The most direct public competitor is [Credo Technology Group](https://www.credosemi.com/) (CRDO), whose Active Electrical Cable and Active Optical Cable products address substantially the same end-market position. The competitive dynamic between Astera Taurus and Credo's cable module business is the clearest public read-across available for understanding Taurus's market share trajectory, given the absence of segment-level revenue disclosure from either company.

At 800G — the speed at which the hyperscalers pushing next-generation GPU cluster deployments are deploying new inter-rack fabric — the embedded silicon differentiation of smart cable modules becomes more defensible: passive solutions face genuine physics constraints at those line rates and link lengths, and the monitoring capability reduces operational costs in large-scale deployments. Astera has positioned Taurus as the connectivity silicon for AI scale-out networks, and the product family's revenue trajectory through 2025 reflected the broader build-out of AI cluster networking infrastructure that accompanied Blackwell deployment.

## Leo: CXL memory expansion and the disaggregation option

Leo is the CXL memory expansion controller, and it is categorically different from Aries and Taurus in its revenue maturity and its strategic positioning. The product family addresses the memory bandwidth and capacity wall that large-model AI inference and training workloads expose in conventional server designs: a CPU socket can only directly address a finite amount of DRAM, and as GPU accelerators require larger memory pools for model weights and KV-cache, attaching additional memory via the CXL.mem protocol on the PCIe Gen5 fabric provides an architectural path to larger effective memory capacity without redesigning the accelerator itself.

At the FY2025 disclosure level, Leo was smaller revenue than Aries or Taurus. Its strategic importance is larger than its current revenue contribution implies. The hyperscaler-scale deployment of CXL memory expansion is gated on the availability of CXL-capable host CPUs at volume — primarily Intel's Sapphire Rapids and Granite Rapids server CPUs, and AMD's Genoa and Turin lines — and the software ecosystem maturity for CXL memory tiering. Both conditions have been advancing through 2024-2025, and Leo positions Astera at the intersection of the CXL memory-disaggregation trend and the existing AI server design-in relationships that Aries established. When a hyperscaler that already runs Astera Aries retimers evaluates a CXL memory expansion controller, the qualification path is not starting from scratch.

The competitive framing on Leo is the CXL Consortium standards process itself — memory expansion controller architectures are not proprietary in the way GPU interconnects are, so the differentiation is execution quality, diagnostic capability, and the design-in advantage that comes from an established connectivity-silicon supplier relationship.

## Scorpio: the fabric switch and the NVLink question

Scorpio is the most strategically consequential product family in Astera's portfolio, and also the least revenue-material at the FY2025 snapshot. It is a PCIe/CXL fabric switch — the silicon that enables multiple GPU accelerators to be connected through an open-standard PCIe/CXL fabric rather than through Nvidia's proprietary NVLink/NVSwitch interconnect. In an eight-GPU server node, the standard design uses either NVSwitch silicon (for Nvidia DGX-style systems) or PCIe switch silicon to handle the GPU-to-GPU traffic that model-parallel training and inference requires. Scorpio addresses the PCIe switch position with CXL-aware fabric capability, enabling disaggregated GPU memory and compute configurations that proprietary NVSwitch architectures cannot support.

The strategic option value in Scorpio is the architecture-level bet that not all hyperscaler AI server designs will remain anchored to NVLink. Microsoft, Meta, Google, and Amazon have each invested in custom AI silicon programs — Cobalt/Maia, MTIA, TPU, Trainium/Inferentia — and none of those programs uses NVSwitch. The PCIe/CXL fabric switch market for non-Nvidia-ecosystem AI servers is a genuine addressable market that Broadcom and Marvell have also approached through different product architectures. Astera's Scorpio product is the most direct challenge to the structural assumption that GPU interconnect fabric belongs to the GPU vendor.

The competitive risk is asymmetric: if Nvidia continues to expand NVLink domain sizes and hyperscalers continue to purchase Nvidia GPU clusters in HGX/DGX form factors that come pre-equipped with NVSwitch, Scorpio's addressable market is bounded by the share of AI server deployments that route outside the Nvidia ecosystem. That share has been growing, but Nvidia's volume dominance in FY2025 AI infrastructure spending was not in dispute.

## The margin architecture

The 75.7% GAAP gross margin that Astera reported for FY2025 — consistent within 10 basis points across the quarterly prints — is the number that most distinguishes this business from a conventional fabless semiconductor company. [Astera Labs FY2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001736297/000173629726000010/alab-20251231.htm) shows this level sustained through a year in which revenue more than doubled.

The structural explanation has three components. First, the design-in economics: an 18-24 month hyperscaler qualification cycle, once won, generates revenue without price renegotiation at the cadence of a competitive tender. Customers who have qualified Astera silicon into a platform generation cannot practically switch mid-cycle without absorbing months of requalification work and the associated schedule risk in a capital-expenditure cycle where schedule is the most constrained variable. Second, the process-node economics: Aries PCIe Gen5 and Gen6 retimers require leading-edge analog SerDes IP at advanced TSMC nodes, and Astera's volume in FY2025 — over $850M of revenue from a single fab supplier — provides negotiating leverage on wafer pricing and OSAT terms that is unavailable to smaller competitors. Third, the IP architecture: the majority of Astera's cost structure is engineering, tape-out amortization, and the sustaining costs of the design teams that maintain and extend the product families. Physical goods cost — wafer, assembly, test — is a smaller fraction of revenue than it would be for a memory company or a higher-complexity SoC supplier.

## Concentration, not diversification

The revenue map across the four product families shares a single terminal destination: the AI server and rack. There is no meaningful revenue diversification into edge compute, automotive, or non-AI enterprise server markets visible in the FY2025 disclosure. Aries flows into AI server GPU-to-CPU signal paths. Taurus flows into AI cluster inter-rack Ethernet. Leo flows into AI server CXL memory expansion. Scorpio flows into AI infrastructure PCIe/CXL fabric builds. The diversification within the connectivity-silicon product stack — four technically distinct families, three distinct protocol/standards ecosystems — is real, but it is diversification across the AI infrastructure stack, not diversification away from it.

This concentration is a structural condition, not a near-term remediation target. The FY2025 result was produced by being maximally aligned with the single largest capital-expenditure cycle in enterprise technology history. The risk carried by that alignment is commensurate: a sustained pause in AI infrastructure spending, or a generation-transition miss in design-in position, flows through to Astera with no offset from diversified end-markets. The Q1 2026 guidance midpoint of $291.5M — implying approximately 7.7% sequential growth from a $270.6M Q4 base — suggested that, as of the guidance date, the AI infrastructure spend cycle remained intact.
